---
applyTo: "api/**"
---

# API Coding Conventions

## REST Controllers

- `create*` handlers historically destructure only specific fields off the request body (e.g. `const { dogs, description, position } = req.body`) before building the document, while `update*` handlers spread the whole payload (`{ ...data }`) into `findOneAndUpdate`. Adding a new field to an entity and only wiring it into the form/type layer silently drops it on create — the field never reaches `Model.create(...)` unless it's added to the destructure too. Check every `create*` handler's destructure when adding a field, not just the corresponding `update*` handler.
- This asymmetry exists because `findOneAndUpdate(filter, { ...data }, ...)` is safe to spread — Mongoose treats a plain object update as an implicit `$set`, so fields absent from `data` are left untouched rather than wiped. `create*` has no such safety net: whatever isn't explicitly destructured never exists on the new document.

## Deletion cascades (orphaned-reference cleanup)

Most entities are denormalized somewhere else in the schema (a full embedded copy, e.g. `Task.dogs`, `Team.dogs`/`matchups[].dogs`, `User.dogs`, `crossPass.runningOnDog`; or a lightweight `{_id, status}` reference, e.g. `Event.dogs[]`/`Event.users[]`; or an ID pair, e.g. `Task.matchupRef.squadId/matchupId`). Deleting or editing the source document does **not** automatically fix these — every embedded/referenced copy goes stale or dangling unless the delete/update handler explicitly cascades. Decided cascade behavior, per entity:

- **Dog** update/delete → `api/src/helpers/dogCascade.js`'s `replaceDogEverywhere(club, dogId, replacement)`. On update, refreshes the dog's embedded copy in `Task.dogs`, `Team.dogs`, every `Team.matchups[].dogs`, `User.dogs`, and `crossPass.runningOnDog` (both the standalone `CrossPass` collection and embedded `Team.matchups[].crossPasses`). On delete (`replacement = null`): removes the dog from all of those, **and** deletes any `CrossPass`/lineup-cross-pass entry the dog *owns* (`dogId` match — a leg is meaningless without its runner), **and** clears (not deletes) any entry where the dog was the *predecessor* (`runningOnDog`).
  - Intentionally left dangling: `Event.dogs[]` attendance entries. A deleted dog just silently disappears from the UI (display iterates the live Dogs list, not the stale attendance array) — not worth the churn.
- **Team**/**Lineup** delete → `api/src/helpers/lineupCascade.js`'s `detachTasksFromMatchup(club, squadId, matchupId, dogs)`. Any `Task.matchupRef` pointing at the removed team/lineup gets the ref cleared **and** the lineup's last-known `dogs` snapshotted into the task's own `dogs` array, so the task keeps working standalone instead of pointing at nothing. Note there's no dedicated "delete lineup" endpoint — a lineup disappears via a normal `PATCH /teams` whose `matchups` array is just missing it, so `teamController.js`'s `updateTeam` diffs old vs. new `matchups` to detect this.
  - Intentionally left dangling: `Event.users[]` attendance entries on **User** delete (same reasoning/consistency as dog attendance above).
- **Dog removed from a team's pool** (`Team.dogs`, via the same `PATCH /teams`) → `lineupCascade.js`'s (pure) `keepOnlyPoolDogsInMatchups(matchups, allowedDogIds)`. There's no dedicated endpoint for this either — every lineup in the team gets scrubbed to only reference dogs still in `data.dogs`: removed from `lineup.dogs`, any cross-pass entry a disallowed dog *owns* deleted, any entry where it was the *predecessor* cleared (not deleted) — same two rules as the Dog-delete cascade above, just scoped to one team instead of the whole club. This one was a deliberate product decision (dogs leaving the pool follow into lineups), not the "leave lineups as independent snapshots" behavior that governs team/lineup *deletion* above — don't conflate the two.
  - **This function is keyed off the payload's own `dogs` list ("allowed"), not a diff against the pre-update DB state ("removed") — deliberately, after a real incident.** An earlier version computed `removedDogIds` by diffing against `existingTeam`; a double-click before the first request's response updated the UI fired a second overlapping `PATCH /teams` built from a stale snapshot, and the second request's diff (against a DB state the first request had *already* changed) silently resurrected a dog the first request had just removed. Keying off `data.dogs` directly makes every save independently self-correcting regardless of request ordering. If you add another "diff old vs new" cascade, consider whether it needs the same "invariant of the payload" treatment instead of a state diff — anywhere a double-submit is plausible (i.e. any user-facing async button with no loading/disabled state), a diff-based cascade is a landmine.
- **User**, **Event**, **DogTask**, **CrossPass**, **Task**, **EventTemplate** deletes: nothing else in the schema references these by ID (Task.description is a free-text string, not a DogTask reference; EventTemplate.tasks is an immutable snapshot, not a live link) — no cascade exists or is needed.

**Critical gotcha**: `superAdminController.js`'s generic `updateItem`/`deleteItem` (the super-admin entity grid) is a **second, independent write path** for every entity — it does not call through `dogController.js`/`teamController.js` at all. Any cascade wired into a dedicated controller must *also* be special-cased into `updateItem`/`deleteItem` (see the `entity === "dogs"` / `entity === "teams"` branches there) or the super-admin grid silently bypasses it and reintroduces the exact orphaned-reference bug. When adding a new embedded/denormalized relationship, or a new cascade to an existing one, put the logic in a shared `api/src/helpers/*Cascade.js` module and wire it into *both* places — never duplicate the logic inline in one controller only.

## Cross-entity propagation on update (not just deletion)

Not every fan-out is about cleanup — some propagate a value *forward*. Two independent opt-in flags on `Dog`, both toggled from the user's Settings page (a super admin, having no dogs of their own, picks any club dog(s) from a multi-select instead), both living in `api/src/helpers/crossPassSync.js`:

- **`Dog.syncCrossPasses`** — lineup ↔ lineup. `syncCrossPassTiming` copies a lineup cross-pass's `note`/`startingPosition`/`time` (never the pairing itself — `dogId`/`runningOnDog`/`runningOnLights` stay put) to every *other* lineup entry (any team in the club) with the same dog + same predecessor ("same predecessor → same timing").
- **`Dog.syncCrossPassesWithMyDogs`** — lineup ↔ standalone `CrossPass` (the My Dogs page), independently toggleable from the flag above. **Bidirectional, and asymmetric in what it's allowed to create**:
  - Lineup → My Dogs (`syncCrossPassesToMyDogs`, called from the team-update path): **upserts** a matching standalone `CrossPass` — creates one from scratch if none exists yet, since the My Dogs list is free-form.
  - My Dogs → lineup (`syncCrossPassFromMyDogs`, called from `crossPassController.js`'s `createCrossPass`/`updateCrossPass`): reuses `syncCrossPassTiming` itself, but **update-only** — a lineup's cross-pass "slots" are fixed by that lineup's dog running order, so unlike the other direction there's no valid new row to fabricate on this side.

`findChangedSyncedCrossPasses` diffs the incoming `PATCH /teams` payload against the pre-update team to find entries that actually changed (so it doesn't do a no-op rewrite on every save), and tags each with `syncLineups`/`syncMyDogs` booleans read off that dog's two flags — callers must filter by the relevant flag before invoking the matching sync function (`syncCrossPassTiming` doesn't filter internally, since it's also reused ad-hoc for the My-Dogs→lineup direction where there's no entry list to filter). The two DB-touching sync functions (`syncCrossPassTiming`, `syncCrossPassesToMyDogs`) each wrap a **pure** counterpart (`applyCrossPassSyncToTeams`, `buildMyDogsSyncOps`) that takes plain data in and returns bulkWrite ops out with no DB access — that's the seam the unit tests in `crossPassSync.test.js` exercise; follow the same split (pure diff/compute function wrapped by a thin DB-calling function) for any new propagation logic, so it stays testable without mongodb-memory-server.

Same double-wiring rule as the deletion cascades above: the lineup-side sync calls live in both `teamController.js`'s `updateTeam` and `superAdminController.js`'s `entity === "teams"` branch.

## Testing

`yarn test` (Vitest) runs two kinds of tests, and it matters which one a given piece of logic needs:

- **Pure-logic unit tests** (`*.test.js` next to the helper, e.g. `crossPassSync.test.js`, `lineupCascade.test.js`) — no DB, no mocking. Every cascade/propagation helper is split into a thin DB-calling function plus a pure counterpart that takes plain objects in and returns plain data (bulkWrite ops, diff results, etc.) out; these tests exercise only the pure half. Fast, and this is where most of the actual branching logic lives — write these first for any new pure function.
- **Integration tests** (`*.integration.test.js`, e.g. `teamController.integration.test.js`) — a real (ephemeral, in-memory) MongoDB via `mongodb-memory-server`, wired up once in `vitest.setup.js` (spun up in a global `beforeAll`, collections wiped in `afterEach`, torn down in `afterAll`). These call the actual exported controller functions directly with a plain `{club, body/params}` req and the `mockRes()` helper from `src/testHelpers.js` — no real HTTP/Express, no mocking of Mongoose. **This is the only reliable way to test a controller in this codebase**: `vi.mock()` does not intercept the plain CommonJS `require()` calls controllers use to load models (confirmed by trying it — the "mocked" model was silently bypassed and the real code tried to hit a real MongoDB connection instead). If you need to test that a controller *calls* the right helpers with the right arguments (wiring, not just behavior), write an integration test, not a mock-based one.
- When asserting on a field that a cascade `$unset`s (e.g. `Task.matchupRef`), assert against `doc.toJSON()`/`doc.toObject()`, not the raw Mongoose Document. A `$unset` on a plain nested-object path (not a real sub-`Schema`) leaves the in-memory Document showing an empty shell (e.g. `{ squadId: undefined, matchupId: undefined }`), which is truthy and has no keys removed — Mongoose's default `minimize` behavior only strips that down to nothing during serialization (`.toJSON()`/`.toObject()`, i.e. what an API response actually sends). Testing the raw property gives a false failure; testing the serialized form matches what the frontend actually receives.
- There's a permanent regression test for the actual production incident that motivated the integration-test setup: `src/importsMatchExports.test.js` statically walks every local `require(...)` in `api/src` and asserts every destructured name is really exported by that module. It exists because `node --check` is pure syntax checking — it can't catch a destructure of a name that no longer exists on the required module (that silently evaluates to `undefined`, only throwing once something actually *calls* it, which for a route handler means "the first real request after deploy"). This is exactly what happened: `lineupCascade.js`'s `removeDogsFromMatchups` was renamed to `keepOnlyPoolDogsInMatchups`, but its two callers weren't updated until the next `PATCH /teams` in production threw. Don't rely on `node --check` alone to catch a rename — either run the test suite (it would have failed immediately) or grep for the old name across the whole controllers/ and helpers/ tree before considering a rename done.
